In terms of weight loss:

In semaglutide, it’s largely just changing appetite and satiety. A big calories in adjustment. 

In tirzepatide, it also changes appetite and cravings, and also fat oxidation but not to the extent that it changes energy expenditure (calories out). When you lose weight, your energy expenditure (EE) usually drops as your weight decreases, which is called metabolic adaptation. In a mouse study with tirzepatide, they found it attenuated metabolic adaptation meaning that it reduced the amount that the energy expenditure dropped, but in tests on humans, the energy expenditure drop remained proportional to what those who lost weight on placebo experienced - so no change to metabolic adaptation.

I believe Novo has run experiments on CagriSema showing a more pronounced reduction in metabolic adaptation in rats, but it remains to be seen if that will translate to humans.

Lilly has also run human a human trial much like the tirzepatide EE trial for the upcoming retatrutide, but they have not released those results yet.  Because Reta adds glucagon, it’s anticipated there will be an EE change in those results, but results are TBD. Hopefully Lilly will release that info this summer.

They all certainly do adjust other metabolic processes - that’s why they are used to treat a type 2 diabetes, providing better blood sugar control, but that does not appear to meaningfully adjust EE. They also have plenty of other benefits in the kidneys, liver, heart, etc, but that’s outside the weight loss discussion.

With semaglutide going off-patent in the Indian market, we are about to see a massive surge in its usage for both diabetes and obesity. As an ophthalmologist, I believe it is important to look beyond the metabolic benefits and address the fine print that often gets lost in the excitement.

One of the most common complaints we'll likely hear is blurred vision. It is important to educate patients that this is often a refractive shift rather than permanent damage; rapid fluctuations in blood sugar can cause the lens of the eye to swell or shrink, leading to temporary blurring.

We also need to be proactive about drug-induced dry eye disease. Emerging evidence suggests GLP-1 RAs may induce dry eye by altering the production or composition of the tear film. This can lead to a gritty sensation and further blurred vision, which we can help manage with lifestyle modifications or ocular lubricants.

However, the more serious concerns; Nonarteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (NAION) and the early worsening of Diabetic Retinopathy (DR), require attention. While data is mixed, some large cohort studies have shown a threefold higher risk of NAION in semaglutide users. Furthermore, the rapid drop in HbA1c can paradoxically trigger DR progression, likely due to osmotic shifts, altered VEGF signalling, and the breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier.

The real clinical challenge we face is the lack of clear guidelines. While the ADA standards of care advise assessing a patient’s DR status before starting or escalating GLP-1 RA treatment, they do not specify how often follow-up eye exams should be performed in this specific context.

Given the impending explosion of these prescriptions in India, here is my approach:
Baseline retinal evaluation: We must know the state of the retina before the rapid glycemic shift begins.
High risk eyes: Patients with pre-existing severe NPDR or proliferative DR need much tighter monitoring.
Patient education: We must teach patients to distinguish between temporary refractive blur and the sudden, painless vision loss associated with NAION.

Don’t make a meal of your business lunch. Here are 20 rules that’ll help you avoid a two-course ordeal

A business lunch can be a fine thing. Over a couple of courses, you can find common ground, show your appreciation and navigate what might have seemed like a tricky relationship when it was all taking place online. But after years of video calls and working from home, people have grown shy of the idea. So here’s a starter pack of advice.
1.
You will probably have between an hour and 90 minutes so ensure that you choose the restaurant wisely. Tasting menus and wine pairings are painful at the best of times. At lunch, they are like a kidnapping with compote. Oh, and no sharing concepts.

2.
The restaurant should be easy to find. Your counterparts shouldn’t need the skills of Sir Ranulph Fiennes to locate “this really cool place that I’ve heard about”. You want this friendship – meet in the middle and respect their time.

3.
Don’t be scared to go low. It won’t work every time but sometimes modesty is the best policy. Fish and chips? Why not?

4.
No laptops or phones. It’s a restaurant, not the Apple Store.

5.
An emergency call from the office? You may go outside once. But you are already losing the room. Twice? It will look as though you’re having an affair or are just rude.
📷

6.
Know your neighbours. Don’t wander into sensitive territory and ask financial questions if half of the people in the club or restaurant are in the same trade as you. And if the key numbers can’t be written down on the back of a napkin, don’t attempt to pick apart spreadsheet-level details while dissecting a guinea fowl.

7.
Arrive on time. Sorry, I don’t care if your husband lost a leg this morning. The clock is ticking.

8.
Here are the lateness rules. Ten minutes are forgivable (ask the maître d’ for a newspaper or have an emergency novel in your pocket; don’t just scroll). Twenty minutes late? They’re paying. Thirty minutes? Have a nice lunch and finish your book.

9.
Be interesting. The best business lunches are with people who know stuff and can tell a story or two. No, they don’t want to see pictures of your children.

10.
Shut up. Listen. It’s a rare skill but one you should perfect.

11.
If you are American, don’t look horrified when a European orders a glass of wine at lunch. No intervention is needed.

12.
If you’re jabbing your thigh with semaglutide these days and have the appetite of a dormouse, why did you come? As soon as you asked the waiter if they could do a half-portion of the rocket salad, this was over.

13.
“I won’t have bread but if you want it, please go ahead.” Really, avoid all virtue signalling when ordering. Show that you’re the kind of person who knows how to let everyone get what they want from an agreement – even when it’s just the breadbasket that’s at stake. 

14.
Be decent. That means to the restaurant staff too. At the end of a very nice lunch this week, my guest said to the waiter, “Your service has been exceptional. Indeed, it was a highlight of the meal.” It was one of those small interactions that underlined why I love working with this writer.

15.
How many courses? Having just a starter and a main is the industry standard. Just a main is also fine, though it can imply that you would rather be out of there. Puddings? They can work but the lunch now risks resembling a family outing with grandma.

16.
Coffee? Ordering espressos with the bill will leave everyone feeling caffeinated and on schedule. “Can I have a pot of your green tea?” is a sentence that will cause anxiety levels to rise among your fellow diners.

17.
Who’s paying? Splitting a bill for a business lunch is rarely wise. If you’re the one who selected the venue and set the dining pace, just pay. If your counterpart has been ascending to the Himalayan heights of the wine menu or ordering a labrador-sized steak, sit back.
 
18.
No doggy bags. You might not like to waste food but unless you’re working for an NGO, taking away a tub of slowly congealing dauphinoise potatoes won’t make you look cool, just parsimonious.

19.
They paid? Say thank you. 

20.
You paid? Say thank you for their time and for being good company. Well, only if they were.

A recent study from University of Cambridge researchers, published in eClinicalMedicine, raises serious red flags about what happens when people stop GLP-1 medications like Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, or Zepbound after major weight loss.
The analysis drew from six rigorous randomized trials involving over 3,200 participants. The results are alarming:
• Within just one year of stopping, people regain about 60% of the weight they lost.
• Over longer periods, regain can climb to as much as 75%, with most of it returning within roughly 60 weeks.
• Only about 25% of the initial loss seems to stay off long-term.
Even more disturbing is the impact on body composition: 40–60% of the weight lost on these drugs often comes from lean muscle mass, not just fat.
When the weight rebounds—and it usually does—it comes back primarily as fat.
This leaves many people in a worse spot than before: higher body fat percentage, reduced muscle, weakened metabolism, lower strength, and increased long-term health risks, including greater vulnerability to conditions like sarcopenia in older adults.
High discontinuation rates compound the problem—around half of users stop within the first year due to intolerable side effects, high costs, or access barriers—triggering this rapid, often devastating rebound.
These drugs can deliver impressive short-term results for obesity and type 2 diabetes, affecting over a billion people worldwide.
But the evidence shows they're far from a simple or safe fix.
Without aggressive countermeasures—like resistance training, high protein intake, and sustained lifestyle changes—muscle loss accelerates, and stopping the drug frequently undoes progress while leaving lasting damage.
If you're on these medications or considering them, insist on a detailed discussion with your doctor: body composition monitoring, strength-focused exercise plans, and a realistic strategy for maintenance or safe discontinuation.
Beyond the rebound and muscle wasting, other reported concerning side effects include persistent gastrointestinal issues (severe nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation), gallbladder problems (gallstones, cholecystitis), pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas, which can be life-threatening and has led to reported deaths), potential risks of thyroid tumors or cancer (noted in animal studies and carrying FDA boxed warnings, though human evidence remains inconclusive), kidney issues, vision problems like non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), and more.
In light of the rapid regain, significant muscle loss, high dropout rates, and these additional serious risks, the risks are rarely worth the benefits for most people seeking sustainable weight management.

By William Wallace, PhD.

The "Quarter Rule" in body composition research holds that roughly 25% of weight lost during calorie restriction comes from lean mass rather than fat. This ratio has been consistent across meta-analyses of dietary interventions and holds for bariatric surgery in a similar range (~20-24% depending on procedure type).

DXA substudies from the major GLP-1 and GLP-1/GIP trials show most incretin therapies landing in the same neighborhood. Tirzepatide (SURMOUNT-1, 72 weeks) produced 21.3% total body weight loss with 26% of that loss attributable to lean mass.

Liraglutide came in at 16% in a smaller cohort (6 months). Both figures fall within the expected range for any equivalent calorie deficit.

Semaglutide is the notable exception. In the STEP 1 DXA substudy (68 weeks), 40% of total weight lost was lean mass. Other semaglutide datasets report lower figures (the COURAGE trial measured ~35%), suggesting 40% may represent the upper bound, but even the lower estimates exceed the diet-only benchmark.

An important measurement caveat: DXA quantifies "lean body mass," which includes water, organ tissue, and connective tissue in addition to skeletal muscle. A portion of measured lean loss reflects adaptive tissue remodeling during weight reduction, not direct muscle catabolism.

All trials included lifestyle counseling, but none required resistance training or set specific protein targets. A recent case series of patients who combined incretin therapy with resistance training (3-5 sessions/week) and protein intakes ranging from 0.7-1.7 g/kg/day found that one patient lost 6.9% lean mass despite 33% total weight loss, and two patients with higher protein intakes actually gained lean mass while losing 13-27% of body weight.

The irony of this conversation is that the people most alarmed about GLP-1 muscle loss are fitness-conscious people who already lift and eat adequate protein. They are the least likely to have a "problem". The people at actual risk are sedentary patients with low baseline protein intake and no training history. They are probably not reading this post.

GLP-1s produce substantially more total weight loss than calorie restriction alone, which means more absolute lean mass is lost. But for most of these drugs, the proportional ratio is not meaningfully different from dieting. The clinical variable that appears to matter most is not which drug is prescribed but whether the prescribing protocol includes resistance training and adequate protein intake alongside it.

Yes, energy balance matters. No one disputes that. But the body is not a passive furnace where calories go in and heat comes out. It’s a hormonal system that actively regulates hunger, energy expenditure, and fat storage.

We’ve known for decades that genetics influence body weight. Twin and adoption studies consistently show 40–70% heritability of BMI. And specific variants such as those in the FTO gene affect appetite regulation and energy balance.

More importantly, when people lose weight the body fights back. Hormones change:
•Leptin drops
•Ghrelin rises
•Resting metabolic rate decreases

This phenomenon—called adaptive thermogenesis—is why long-term weight maintenance is difficult even for highly disciplined people.

That’s also why modern treatments like Semaglutide and Tirzepatide work. They change the hormonal signals that regulate hunger and metabolism. If obesity were simply a “discipline problem,” these medications wouldn’t produce the large, reproducible weight loss seen in randomized trials.

So the short version:

Calories matter.
But biology decides how hungry you are, how efficiently you burn those calories, and how hard your body fights weight loss.

Calling that “just discipline” is not physiology. It’s moralizing.
